headline: The Social Work Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet patients and families, give times and numbers, ask simple questions about home, money and support, and make polite requests, and start Social Work Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Greet patients and families politely and say basic hospital words with clear Spanish sounds.
lessons.focus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr, silent h and the written accent; greetings

words.note: A man is el trabajador social. The j sounds like English h.
A woman is la paciente. Each e sounds like 'eh'.
Every a sounds like 'ah', and i like 'ee'.
The h is silent: 'os-pee-TAL'.
ll sounds like English y: 'ya-MA-da'.
ch sounds like English ch in 'check'.
Silent h; j sounds like English h: 'EE-ho'.
rr is a strong trilled r.
The written accent shows the stressed syllable: te-LÉ-fo-no.
u sounds like 'oo'.

words.en: Good morning, my name is Ana.

words.note: Formal, for patients and families. With a coworker: ¿Cómo estás?

words.en: Good afternoon, I'm from the social work department.
words.es: Buenas tardes, soy del departamento de trabajo social.
Hasta mañana, que le vaya bien.

lessons.speaking: Greet a patient in their hospital room, say your name, say you are from social work, and ask how they are.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say ages, times, days and dollar amounts a patient or family gives you during a visit.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time, and days, months, dollars and household size

words.note: Write the ñ: año means year; ano is a different word.

words.en: There are 4 of us in the house.

words.note: Spanish uses tener for age: 'I have 67 years'.

words.en: You leave the hospital in 2 days.
words.es: Usted sale del hospital en 2 días.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient their age, how many people live at home and their monthly income, then tell them the time of their appointment.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who you are and describe how a patient feels or where a family member is.
lessons.focus: ser for who someone is, estar for feelings, conditions and location

words.note: For a woman: sola.
For a woman: preocupada.
For a woman: cansada.
Estar listo means ready; ser listo means smart.
Use estar casado in everyday speech.
For a woman: enferma.
A man is el enfermero.
A man is el doctor.

words.es: Soy la trabajadora social del hospital.
words.note: ser: who you are. A man says Soy el trabajador social.

words.es: Mi esposo está en el cuarto 12.
words.note: estar: location.

words.en: I'm very worried about my house.
words.es: Estoy muy preocupada por mi casa.
words.note: estar: a feeling that can change. A man says preocupado.

words.en: Are you ready to leave today?

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient who you are, then ask if they feel worried, tired or calm and where their family member is.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Ask what a patient has and needs at home: housing, food, transportation and a caregiver.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive

words.note: Common in US Spanish; el alquiler is also understood.
A man is el cuidador.

words.en: Do you have a safe place to live?
I need help with the rent.
Is there someone at home to take care of you?
words.note: cuidarlo for a man, cuidarla for a woman.

words.en: I want to talk with my daughter.
You have to fill out the form before leaving.
words.es: Hay que llenar el formulario antes de salir.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: something that must be done.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient if they have housing, a car and health insurance, and what they need at home after the hospital.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Talk about where a patient will go after discharge and what they can do on their own.
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer and poder

words.note: In Mexico people also say el camión.
la mañana means the morning.
Use el for 'on': el lunes = on Monday.
dar de alta = to discharge a patient from the hospital.

words.en: I'm going to call your daughter.
words.es: Voy a llamar a su hija.
words.note: Use the personal a before a person: llamar a su hija.

words.en: Can you go to the clinic by bus?
words.es: ¿Puede ir en autobús a la clínica?

words.en: Tomorrow we're going to make the discharge plan.
words.es: Mañana vamos a hacer el plan de alta.

words.en: I'll make you an appointment for Monday.
words.es: Le hago una cita para el lunes.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient what you are going to do for their discharge and ask if they can get to the clinic or pharmacy.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Ask and answer simple questions about who a patient lives with, works with and talks to.
lessons.focus: Present tense -ar, -er, -ir endings for yo, tú, usted, nosotros and ellos

words.note: los hijos means one's own sons and daughters.
A woman is la vecina.

words.en: Do you live with your family?
I live with my wife and my children.
words.es: Vivo con mi esposa y mis niños.

words.note: Informal tú, for a coworker. To a patient: ¿Habla español?

words.en: My neighbor helps me with food.
words.es: Mi vecina me ayuda con la comida.
Nosotros llamamos a la clínica mañana.
words.note: The present tense can describe a near-future plan.

words.es: Mis hijos trabajan todo el día.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient who they live with, who helps them, and whether their family works or speaks English.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask a patient the basic who, what, where, when and how-much questions of an intake.
lessons.focus: Question words: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: Agrees with the noun: cuánta, cuántos, cuántas.
Two words with an accent; porque (one word) means because.
Use ¿Cuál es...? for a name, address or number.

words.en: Where are you going to live after the hospital?
words.es: ¿Dónde va a vivir después del hospital?

words.en: Who takes care of you at home?
words.note: lo for a man, la for a woman.

words.en: How much do you pay in rent per month?
Why can't you go back home?
words.es: ¿Por qué no puede volver a casa?

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient their name, date of birth and address, where they will live after the hospital, and who takes care of them.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Understand when a patient says they have no one, nothing, or not enough money yet.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos and otro

words.note: Spanish uses a double negative: No tengo nada.
For a feminine noun: otra. Never say 'un otro'.

words.en: I don't have anywhere to live.
I don't have health insurance yet.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient if anyone helps at home and if they have money for food, and listen for no, nobody, never and not yet.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Politely ask a patient to sign, bring documents, sit down or wait.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede…? requests and usted commands: firme, llene, traiga, siéntese, espere

words.note: Common in Mexico; el bolígrafo is also understood.
Usted command: llenar becomes llene.

words.es: Traiga su identificación mañana, por favor.

words.en: Can you give me your phone number?
words.es: ¿Me puede dar su número de teléfono?

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient politely to sit down, fill out and sign a form, and bring their ID and insurance card next time.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize social work cognates and ask for help, repetition or an interpreter.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad, -ente, and survival phrases for getting help

words.note: salud means health; it is not a cognate.
A woman is la intérprete.

words.en: I don't understand, can you repeat, please?
I'm going to get an interpreter.
words.es: Voy a buscar a un intérprete.

words.en: How do you say "housing" in Spanish?
It's an emergency, I need help.

lessons.speaking: Tell a family member you don't understand, ask them to speak more slowly, and say you are going to get an interpreter.
